rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Dot product is just multiplication of magnitudes — Dot product is $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, NOT just $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$. The cosine factor accounts for direction. If $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$, the dot product is 0 even though both are non-zero.  ·  Dot product is commutative only sometimes — Dot product is ALWAYS commutative: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$. There are no exceptions for non-zero vectors.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: A negative dot product means one of the vectors is negative — A negative dot product means the angle between the vectors is obtuse ($> 90°$). Both vectors can be entirely positive (e.g., 5 N and 10 N at 120° give $-25$).  ·  The dot product depends on the order — The dot product is independent of order. $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$. Only the cross product has order dependence.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The dot product was introduced by **Hermann Grassmann** in 1844 and independently by **William Kingdon Clifford** in 1878. It is the foundation of the **inner product** in linear algebra, generalizing to higher dimensions.  ·  **Work-energy theorem** in its vector form: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = \Delta K$. The dot product of force and displacement gives the work, which equals the change in kinetic energy.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Definition**: the scalar product (or dot product) of two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between them ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$). The result is a scalar quantity.  ·  **Geometric interpretation**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = a(b\cos\theta) = b(a\cos\theta)$ — the product of one vector's magnitude and the projection of the other onto it. If $\theta < 90°$, the projection is positive; if $\theta > 90°$, the projection is negative.  ·  **Physical significance**: the dot product of force and displacement gives work: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$. Only the component of force along the displacement does work; perpendicular components contribute nothing.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Scalar and vector products and other topics  ·  Key Formula 5: Important relation in Scalar and vector products  ·  The dot product formula $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$ works for parallel vectors too — Yes, for $\theta=0°$, $\cos0°=1$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab$. The formula is general for all angles.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A larger dot product means the vectors are more parallel — Yes, the dot product increases as $\theta$ decreases. Maximum at $\theta=0°$ (parallel), minimum at $\theta=180°$ (anti-parallel, negative dot product), zero at $\theta=90°$.  ·  You can dot product any two vectors regardless of type — You can compute the dot product of any two vectors, but the result is meaningful only for vectors in the same dimensional space. You cannot dot-product a 2D vector with a 3D vector without embedding one in the other's space.  ·  $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A}$ is the same as $\vec{A}\cdot|\vec{A}|$ — $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = |\vec{A}|^2$ (magnitude squared), not the product of magnitude and magnitude. The dot product of a vector with itself is always a non-negative scalar.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A unit vector has zero magnitude — A unit vector has magnitude EXACTLY 1, not 0. The zero vector $\vec{0}$ has magnitude 0 and indeterminate direction; a unit vector has magnitude 1 and a specific direction.  ·  Every vector is a unit vector — Only vectors with magnitude 1 are unit vectors. A general vector $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i}$ has magnitude 3, not 1. To get a unit vector, you must divide by the magnitude: $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.  ·  There is only one unit vector in space — There are infinitely many unit vectors, one for each direction in space. In 3D, unit vectors form a unit sphere (all vectors of magnitude 1).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Unit vectors add to give a vector with the sum of magnitudes — Unit vectors add via the parallelogram law, considering their direction. $\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ has magnitude $\sqrt{2}$, not 2.  ·  The unit vector is just the direction — The unit vector encodes ONLY the direction, but it is itself a vector (with magnitude 1). Saying 'just the direction' is informal — formally, the unit vector is a vector in 3D space with magnitude 1.  ·  The unit vector $\hat{A}$ equals $\vec{A}$ — $\hat{A}$ equals $\vec{A}$ only if $|\vec{A}| = 1$. For a general vector, $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$, which is the unit vector in the same direction.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Direction cosines are the same as components — Direction cosines are the components of a unit vector. They are the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the coordinate axes, and their squares sum to 1.  ·  A unit vector along an axis is the same as the axis — The unit vector along the x-axis is $\hat{i}$, which has magnitude 1. The x-axis itself is an infinite line, not a vector.  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Scalar and vector products
